list.listitem: Diagnose hypothyroidism with a confirmed elevated TSH (thyroid-stimulating hormone) >10 mIU/L, typically with low free T4 (FT4).. C
Treat primary hypothyroidism with levothyroxine ~1.6–1.7 mcg/kg/day (use ideal body weight in obesity).. A

In adults <50 years without cardiac disease, start full replacement dose; in older adults or those with cardiovascular disease, start low (12.5–25 mcg/day) and titrate Adjust dose every 4–6 weeks to achieve a target TSH ~0.5–4 mIU/L (often 1–3 mIU/L in younger patients).. C
Do not routinely treat subclinical hypothyroidism (TSH 5–10 mIU/L, normal FT4) in nonpregnant adults unless symptomatic, TSH ≥10, or high-risk features present. B

background.definition: Hypothyroidism is a clinical and biochemical condition characterized by insufficient thyroid hormone production to meet physiologic needs. Overt hypothyroidism: elevated TSH with low FT4 (free thyroxine). Subclinical hypothyroidism: elevated TSH with normal FT4..

list.listitem: Women: spontaneous hypothyroidism occurs in 3.5/1000/year (95% confidence interval [CI], 2.8-4.5). This increases to approximately 4.1/1000/year (95% CI, 3.3-5.0) for all causes. Men: approximately 0.6/1000/year. The probability of developing hypothyroidism increases with age.
Individuals with antithyroid antibodies (TPO ab and Tg ab) convert to overt hypothyroidism at approximately 5% to 20% annually.
Primary hypothyroidism is found in approximately 1% to 2% of the general population.
Women are approximately 14 times more likely to have hypothyroid disease than men.
The prevalance of subclinical hypothyroidism is between 8% and 18% in adults >65. The prevalence is higher in women than men.
The estimated prevalence of undiagnosed hypothyroidism in Europe is approximately 5%.
Worldwide: The most common cause of hypothyroidism is iodine deficiency.

United States: more than 95% of overt hypothyroidism is due to chronic autoimmune thyroiditis (CAT), commonly known as Hashimoto's disease. The onset of hypothyroidism generally occurs a few years to decades following the acute inflammatory phase.

Additional causes of hypothyroidism (in decreasing frequency): surgical thyroidectomy, radioactive iodine (RAI) ablation, external irradiation, infiltrative disease or tumor, and drugs (e.g., amiodarone, lithium).
Hypothyroidism results from insufficient circulating thyroid hormone (T4 and T3) due to primary failure of the thyroid gland (most common) or central causes (pituitary or hypothalamic dysfunction)
Normal thyroid hormone production requires iodine organification via thyroid peroxidase (TPO)
In autoimmune thyroiditis, TPO antibodies (± thyroglobulin antibodies) impair hormone synthesis and lead to progressive gland destruction
Medications may impair thyroid function by inhibiting hormone synthesis (e.g., amiodarone) and altering TSH secretion
Central hypothyroidism results from impaired TSH production due to pituitary or hypothalamic disease

Subclinical hypothyroidism is associated with: Increased risk of progression to overt disease Possible association with cardiovascular disease (mortality benefit from treatment not clearly established)
There is some association between coronary heart disease and subclinical hypothyroidism, although increased mortality has not been demonstrated.
Medical chart review of Scandenavian pathology registry showed a rate of 8% for a diagnosis of hypothyroidism in patients with microscopic colitis.

Risk_Factor.Risk_Name: Personal or family history of autoimmune disease
Elevated TSH and positive antithyroid antibodies—men
Elevated TSH and positive antithyroid antibodies—women

list.listitem: USPSTF states that there is insufficient evidence to recommend for or against routine screening for hypothyroidism in adults. C
Levothyroxine treatment provided no benefit in older persons >65 with subclinical hypothyroidism.
An independent analysis for screening for thyroid disease, based on an extensive literature review, also found insufficient evidence to support population-based screening. C
This analysis did recommend that aggressive case finding is appropriate in pregnant women, women older than 60 years, and others at high risk for thyroid dysfunction. C

The United States Preventive Services Task Force (USPSTF) and American Association of Clinical Endocrinologists (AACE) concluded that there is insufficient evidence to recommend for or against thyroid screening in adults.
The American College of Physicians (ACP) states that it is reasonable to screen women older than 50 years for unsuspected but symptomatic thyroid disease.

An independent analysis of screening for thyroid disease based on an extensive literature review found that there was insufficient evidence to support population-based screening. This analysis did recommend that aggressive case finding is appropriate in pregnant women, women older than 60 years, and others at high risk for thyroid dysfunction. Appropropriate treatment during pregnancy significantly decreases preterm birth, and may decrease miscarriages as well.
Adequate intake of iodine will prevent some forms of hypothyroidism, although insufficient iodine intake is not a problem in the United States.

Patients taking medications that interfere with the production and/or release of thyroxine from the thyroid gland must be followed with serial TSH levels to monitor for early hypothyroidism. Early addition of exogenous thyroxine replacement is recommended.

Patients who have undergone surgical or radioactive iodine treatment of thyroid diseases (eg, Graves' disease, malignancy) are at increased risk for development of overt hypothyroidism. Routine follow up with TSH is required to ensure the patient remains euthyroid.

Women with documented hypothyroidism (taking replacement therapy) who are trying to become pregnant must be closely monitored and it is recommended that their replacement dose of thyroxine be increased by approximately 30% as soon as pregnancy is confirmed.
Current evidence suggest that treatment of preterm infants with nutritional supplement of iodine do not improve mortality or neurodevelopmental outcomes.
Diagnosis is made by a confirmed TSH level >10.0 mU/L with or without associated symptoms. C
Additional tests can include FT4, FT3, thyroid antibodies, thyroid scan, and ultrasonography but these are not required for primary diagnosis. C
Low TSH, in conjunction with low FT4, is consistent with central hypothyroidism and requires evaluation of the hypothalamic-pituitary axis.

Differential.Differential_Features: Similar symptom complex; lethargy, tiredness, no energy, gradual onset but normal TSH
Elevated fasting blood sugar, polyuria, polydipsia
Elevated follicle-stimulating hormone (FSH), decreased estrogen, hot flashes

list.listitem: Gradual symptom onset is typical, with complaints of tiredness, lethargy, cold intolerance, and constipation. Many patients are minimally symptomatic or even asymptomatic.
Symptoms which best rule in hypothyroidism when present are hoarse or hoarser than normal voice, coarser hair, cold intolerance, constipation, and difficulty with math.
Many patients are asymptomatic, especially with subclinical disease

On physical examination, reflex delay with relaxation phase may occur. Best demonstrated in the ankle jerk with patient kneeling backwards in a chair with their legs extended so their feet are suspended in space.
For patients with signs and/or symptoms of hypothyroidism, obtain an TSH; if TSH is >10 mU/L, a repeat TSH or a FT4 (if low) can be obtained to confirm the diagnosis.

If TSH is between 5 and 10 microIU/mL, obtain FT4; if FT4 is in the normal range, a diagnosis of subclinical hypothyroidism is made. The TSH can be obtained every 6 to 12 months to monitor for hypothyroidism. If symptoms develop, treatment may be considered sooner.

ChangingTSH cuttoffs at 0.1 to 0.2 mU/L less than and 1 to 2 mU/L greater than the reference range for reflex testing FreeT4, would reduce need for FreeT 4 testing. This would leave 2.5% of patients with low freeT4 undetected. This would cause minimal effect on clinically relevant cases. Thyroid dysfunction and autoimmune thyroid disease is more prevalent in alopecia areata and screening is encouraged.

Average replacement dose for healthy adults younger than 50 years is 1.7 micrograms/kg body weight per day. The total calculated dose can be initiated at time of diagnosis with appropriate follow up. C

Initiate treatment for older patients and patients with co-morbidity at a fixed dose of 12.5 to 25.0 micrograms/day with increases in dose every 6 to 8 weeks depending on clinical parameters and sensitive TSH (TSH) response. C

Pregnant women using thyroid replacement therapy should have their levothyroxine dose increased by 30% at time of diagnosis of pregnancy and continued through the postpartum period. Return to normal dose after delivery and recheck TSH in 6 weeks. C
Target TSH level with therapy is 1.0 to 3.0 mU/L depending on age and presence/absence of co-morbidities. C
The drug of choice in the average patient with primary hypothyroidism is levothyroxine alone. Use of combination drugs (T4/T3) and desiccated thyroid extract do not offer any advantage. C
Any levothyroxine preparation can be used for replacement therapy. There are no therapeutic differences among common name brand and generic forms of levothyroxine. A
Treatment of subclinical hypothyroidism (TSH 5 - 20 mIU/L and normal thyroxine level) in nonpregnant adults above age 30 years and not at risk for unplanned pregnancy is generally not recommended. B

Patients with a confirmed TSH >10 mU/L should be treated with levothyroxine. Generally, once levothyroxine has been instituted, even at small replacement doses, progression of clinical symptoms is halted; therefore, rapid replacement is not necessary.

The recommended optimal target TSH for healthy patients younger than 50 years is 1.0 to 2.0 mU/L, and for elderly patients and those with co-morbidities is 2.0 to 3.0 mU/L. An TSH level of less than 1.0 mU/L is not optimal and carries the potential risk of adverse cardiac (atrial fibrillation) and metabolic disorders (osteoporosis).

There is no clinical evidence to support one brand of levothyroxine over another, but keep patients on a consistent preparation when possible and recheck TSH after a manufacturer/formulation change.. Desiccated thyroid extract is not recommended as first-line therapy.

For patients with persistent symptoms despite euthyroidism on levothyroxine, a physiologic trial of combination therapy (T4 + T3) may be considered. However, if no clinical improvement is observed after 3 to 6 months, T3 should be discontinued.
The starting dose of levothyroxine is dependent on patient's age, current health, and co-morbidities.

Begin dosing at 25 to 75 micrograms/day with dose increases of 25 to 50 micrograms/day every 6 to 8 weeks. Lower initial doses and increments are appropriate for older patients, and higher ones for young healthy adults. When the daily dose reaches the recommended calculated daily dose (1.7 mcg/kg in young healthy adults, 1.0 mcg/kg in older adults), no additional changes are made until a repeat TSH is obtained in 4 to 6 weeks. At this time, adjustments to the dose are made to obtain the target TSH.

Based on good evidence,a BMJ clinical practice guideline strongly recommends against treating patients with no symptoms or vague symptoms who have a TSH between 10-20 mIU/L. This guideline doesn't apply to patients less than 30 years of age or women at risk of unplanned pregnancy.

With respect to treatment of subclinical hypothyroidism, no studies to date have demonstrated improved outcomes with intervention and recommendations for treatment are based on outcome data from the treatment of overt hypothyroidism. This includes gait speed, muscle strength, and muscle mass., ,
Treatment with levothyroxine in older adults >65 years with subclinical hypothyroidism did not improve mental and physical fatiguability more than placebo.

Similarly, in a RCT of older patients (age >65) with persistent subclinical hypothyroidism treated with thyroid replacement vs placebo, hypothyroid symptoms and tiredness scores improved similarly in treatment and placebo groups.

In a study of 737 adults age 65 years and older with a mean baseline thyrotropin level of 6.4 mIU/L (normal range: 0.4-4.59 mIU/L), one year of levothyroxine therapy started at 50 mcg daily for most patients and gradually increased until their thyrotropin was in the normal range had no clinically significant differences in symptoms, outcome and quality of life was identified after 1 year.
A Swiss placebo-controlled randomized trial in 195 older adults with subclinical hypothyroidism found no effect of levothyroxine treatment on bone density or other measures of bone health.
A study randomizing 95 patients with acute myocardial infarction and subclinical hypothyroidism to levothyroxine or placebo found no effect on left ventricular function one year later.
An RCT showed no difference is systolic and diastolic heart function after treatment with leovothyroxine vs placebo in older adults with mild subclinical hypothyroidism.
In a meta-analysis, treatment of either overt or subclinical hypothyroidism resulted in improved lipid profile, both total cholesterol and hypertriglyceridemia.

The AACE recommends consultation with an endocrinologist in the following situations: (1) patients 18 years or younger; (2) patients unresponsive to therapy; (3) pregnant women; (4) patients with cardiac disease; (5) presence of goiter, nodule, or other structural changes in the thyroid gland; and (6) presence of another endocrine disease.
Complications during treatment of hypothyroidism are rare and generally related to the use of levothyroxine.

The most common complications are insufficient treatment caused by inadequate dosing, poor compliance, or poor absorption (often from polypharmacy). Recommended follow up of TSH levels, patient education, and careful review of medications being used by the patient, including OTC medications, will minimize or eliminate these problems.

The second most common complication is iatrogenic hyperthyroidism due to excessive replacement of thyroxine. This can be minimized by allowing sufficient time (minimum of 4-6 weeks) between TSH levels before adjusting replacement dose, and adjusting the replacement dose of levothyroxine so that the TSH is between 1.0 and 3.0 mU/L.
Hypothyroidism is associated with obstructive sleep apnea; OSA may improve or resolve with thyroid replacement.

In euthyroid individuals with normal TSH, high normal freeT4 levels even inside the range are associated with increase incidence of atrial fibrillation. This is independant of TSH levels. This new information might help physicians evaluate the risk and benefit of dose adjustment of current target thyroid hormones replacement therapy.
Clinical outcomes were similar in patients of atrial fibrillation treated with apixaban vs warfarin, regardless of thyroid disease.

Normalization of TSH level to 1.0 to 3.0 mU/L using levothyroxine replacement therapy, depending on age and presence/absence of co-morbidities, eliminates the adverse clinical signs and symptoms of hypothyroidism. C

Although there is some evidence of improved cardiovascular outcomes following treatment for hypothyroidism, there are no definitive studies demonstrating decreased mortality and morbidity from heart disease in appropriately treated patients. B

A meta-analysis found that primary hypothyroidism is significantly associated with a higher risk and greater severity of metabolic dysfunction-associated steatotic liver disease (MASLD) (OR 1.4 for MASLD and 2.8 for steatohepatitis or advanced fibrosis), independent of levothyroxine replacement.

Untreated hypothyroidism can lead to severe dementia, congestive heart failure, hyperlipidemia, coronary artery disease, hypertension, and death. One clinical case report suggested testing for hypothyroidism (Hashimoto encephalopathy) in patients with Down syndrome and rapidly progressive dementia.
In one study in a Japanese-Brazilian population, subclinical hypothyroidism was an independent risk factor for all-cause mortality.

Subclinical hypothyroidism may also be an independent risk factor for hip and nonspine fractures All the hazard ratios are above one (1.04-2.16) for the risk of fracture from subclinical hypothyroidism; however, the confidence intervals all crossed one.
Hypothyroidism is associated with an increased risk for metabolic dysfunction-associated steatohepatitis.
Long-term prognosis, with maintenance of therapeutic doses of levothyroxine, is excellent. There are no known sequelae or adverse outcomes with appropriately treated hypothyroidism.
Once levothyroxine is initiated, a clinical response can be expected in 1 to 3 weeks when full therapeutic doses are used.
For the young, healthy patient placed on a full therapeutic dose, normalization of TSH can be expected in 1 to 2 months.
For the older patient and those with co-morbidities who are started on a reduced replacement dose, normalization of the TSH may require 3 to 6 months.

Chronic autoimmune thyroiditis is a progressive disease. At time of diagnosis the thyroid gland may still be functioning, albeit at a suboptimal level. As the gland continues to fail, and endogenous thyroxine declines, the replacement dose of levothyroxine will require periodic increases to maintain TSH in the therapeutic range.
Subclinical hypothyroidism is associated with an increased risk of fracture (HR 1.4 for hip fracture, 1.3 for any fracture and 1.2 for non-spine fracture).

Hypothyroidism is accociated with increased all cause mortality instead of cardiovascular mortality in elderly. According to the systematic analysis and meta-analysis, there is considerable heterogeniety and caution is needed interpreting results.
Serum TSH is slow to respond to replacement therapy. A minimum of 4 to 6 weeks following the last change in levothyroxine dose is appropriate.
Obtaining follow-up TSH levels more frequently can result in overtreatment and iatrogenic hyperthyroidism.
When the TSH falls below 5.0 mU/L, the interval for checking TSH levels may be increased to every 3 months.
Once the TSH is stable for two consecutive 6-month cycles, annual TSH determinations are adequate follow up.

A recent retrospective cohort study determined that among patients taking less that 125 mcg of levothyroxine daily who had a stable TSH, fewer than one in 10 will have an abnormal TSH one-year later. In those taking >125 mcg daily the likelihood of an abnrromal TSH within one year goes up to 26.7%.
Routine testing of serum FT4 or FT3 is not necessary for long-term management.

Novel treatment for metastatic prostate cancer by Apalutamide may need survellance for development of hypothyroidism . In a double blind placebo controlled trial 1207 patients. Of which 806 patients assigned to Apalutamide and 401 were assigned to placebo group.Hypothyroidism developed in 8.1% vs 2%. Indicating need for close follow up for new disease diagnosis.
Hypothyroidism is a life-long condition and requires life-long therapy and monitoring.
Levothyroxine has a long half-life, so an occasional missed dose does not result in recurrence of symptoms.
Levothyroxine should be taken daily on an empty stomach, approximately 30 to 60 minutes before breakfast for optimum absorption.
Commonly used drugs that interfere with absorption include antacids, ferrous sulfate, sucralfate, calcium carbonate, cholestyramine, and simethicone.

Patients taking biotin (Vitamin B7) supplements (common in hair/nail formulations) may have falsely low TSH and falsely elevated Free T4 levels due to assay interference. Patients should hold biotin for at least 2 to 3 days prior to thyroid function testing.
Older patients (over 50 years) and patients with known coronary artery disease and/other chronic systemic diseases (eg, diabetes) need special consideration.
Initial therapy with levothyroxine is started at a low dose (12.5-25.0 micrograms daily). Increase the dose by 12.5 to 25.0 micrograms only after a repeat TSH is obtained.
Serial TSH levels should be obtained 6 to 8 weeks after each dose increase, depending on the patient's response to therapy and co-morbidities, to avoid precipitating cardiac events.

In a cross sectional study in Olmsted County, Minnesota, the prevalence of mild cognitive impariment was not associated with thyroid function (euthyroid, subclinical hypothyroid or clinical hypothyroidism).

In a randomized controlled trial (double-blinded) of 737 adults 65 years and older with an elevated TSH (5-1 mIU/L) and normal T4, treatment did not result in any improvement in symptoms. If patients present with a thyrotropin level between 4.6 and 10 mIU/L, repeat the test as the levels often normalize (this occurred in 60% of the patients initially referred for the study) (LOE = 1b).

In a RCT, 65 and older patients with persistent subclinical hypothyroidism when treated with thyroid replacement vs placebo, improved in hypothyroid symptoms and tiredness scores. Here thyroid repalcement was equal to placebo effect.

Hypothyroidism increases the risk of spontaneous abortion. Levothyroxine replacement is essential and early diagnosis is important to decrease this potential complication. Any woman with a history of hypothyroidism and/or taking levothyroxine replacement therapy at the time pregnancy is confirmed should have a TSH obtained as routine.

Pregnancy increases utilization of levothyroxine, therefore patients taking levothyroxine replacement therapy who become pregnant should have their replacement dose increased by 30% empirically. However, there are no outcome studies that have shown this treatment strategy decreases the rate of spontaneous abortion.
After delivery patients return to their prepregnancy levothyroxine dose, with thyroid testing recommended at about 6 weeks postpartum.

Current guidelines recommend an upper limit of normal for TSH of 4.0 mIU/L in the first trimester (unless population-specific ranges are available), replacing the older strict cutoff of 2.5 mIU/L. Treatment targets should aim for the lower half of the trimester-specific reference range.

Among pregnant women with subclinical hypothyroidism (either elevated TSH levels and normal free T4 levels, or normal TSH levels with suppressed T4 levels) treatment with levothyroxine was not associated with significant benefit to offspring IQ with assessments up to 5 years of age, compared to placebo (IQ scores ~94 vs ~97 on the Weschler Preschool and Primary Scale of Intelligence III).
In pregnant women with subclinical hypothyrodism, treatment with levothyroxine did not reduce maternal depressive symptoms. It was somewhat underpowered, though.
An ongoing adjustment approach is as good as emperic dose increase in in maintaning goal TSH in hypothyroid pregnant women.
In one small RCT, levothyroxine therapy to treat pregnant euthyroid women with thyroid peroxidase antibodies reduced that rate of preterm birth by 72% (RR 0.28; 95% CI, 0.10-0.80).

Acute thyroiditis is not uncommon in pregnancy and can be recurrent with subsequent pregnancies. Thyroiditis can have a transient hypothyroid period following the acute phase, with low FT4 and elevated TSH, while the thyroid gland replenishes intraglandular thyroxine stores. Although this process does not represent true hypothyroidism, it can be protracted and, especially in the pregnant woman, should be monitored. Levothyroxine replacement is usually not indicated in acute thyroiditis, but pregnant women who experience this protracted recovery phase, should be followed closely. The threshold to initiate short-term levothyroxine replacement in pregnancy, to ensure adequate circulating thyroxine levels, should be very low.

In one small RCT, use of selenium (Selenomethionine) in women with thyroid autoantibodies decreased the incidence of moderate to advanced postpartum thyroiditis. Measuring TSH, and free T4 between 9 and 14 weeks' gestation, did not predict for adverse pregnancy outcomes in a cohort of 2411 pregnant Australian women.

A meta-analysis of 14 cohort studies involving over 2 million participants concluded that the odds ratio for preterm delivery for pregnant women with overt hypothyroidism was 1.19, and for overt hyperthyroidism was 1.24 when compared to a reference group, an effect not seen with subclinical disease.

A Cochrane review on iodine supplementation for preterm infants concluded that the currently available evidence indicates that routine supplemental iodine did provide have benefits for preterm infants.
Pregnant women without overt thyroid disease but with subclinical hypothyroidism or TPO antibody positivity are at higher risk of preterm birth.
